charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue
segmentRevenue.content:
FIS reports two operating segments plus a residual Corporate and Other bucket that absorbs unallocated costs and runoff. Banking Solutions is core bank processing (deposits, lending, digital banking) and is the larger, steadier segment; Capital Markets Solutions serves buy- and sell-side trading, risk and corporate-liquidity software and has been the faster grower since the Worldpay exit.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: FIS fully exited Worldpay in January 2026, so the three-segment split shown here is the whole company on a continuing basis -- there is no more merchant-acquiring revenue to net out.

What to watch:

  • Capital Markets growing faster than Banking (the mix-shift the market is pricing)
  • Corporate/Other revenue, which is small and mostly a cost allocation, not a growth segment
  • Segment revenue summing back to consolidated Revenue each period

segmentEbitdaMargin.title: Segment Adjusted EBITDA margin
segmentEbitdaMargin.content:
Segment Adjusted EBITDA is management's own profitability measure for each segment -- it excludes the acquisition, integration and transformation charges tied to Issuer Solutions and the Worldpay separation, which this dashboard's owner-FCF DCF charges back in elsewhere. The margin here is segment Adjusted EBITDA divided by segment revenue.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: Banking carries the higher margin of the two; Capital Markets' margin expanding toward it is the operating-leverage case for the segment's faster growth. Corporate/Other is omitted here because it is structurally negative (cost allocation, not a business).

What to watch:

  • Banking margin holding up as the Issuer Solutions integration continues through 2027
  • Capital Markets margin trend versus its revenue growth -- is growth translating into profit
  • Segment Adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP, company-defined measure; it will not tie to consolidated EBITDA elsewhere on this page

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Fidelity National Information Services, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

dcf.base_sublabel: Owner FCF — after SBC, interest income & leases
dcf.model_approach_note: 2026-11-08 one-pass fix per research-stock Step 8c.5. Applied: WACC 8.0% -> 9.0% in all scenarios (+0.5% leverage/refinancing premium, +0.5% regulatory/execution premium; inputs.wacc_rationale). Assessed and NOT applied: mid-cycle FCF rebase (mid_cycle_fcf block: the 839.8 'median' is FY2011 FCF of a company one-third the size; FY2026E owner-FCF margin 14.6% is inside the ten-year 10-15% band). Verified, no change: terminal caps translate to 5.4x / 8.0x / 9.2x adjusted EBITDA (bear/base/bull), all below the ten-year EV/EBITDA minimum of 12.97x (exit_multiple_cap block). No driver path was changed. Residual trip after the fix: implied P/E is 144.9x (down from 163.1x) against a 134.6x threshold. This is a GAAP-earnings denominator artifact, not overvaluation: FY2025 net income (385m) sits roughly 2.6bn below adjusted net income because of about 1.2bn of purchase-accounting amortization from Issuer Solutions and Worldpay, plus acquisition/integration/transformation charges and Worldpay equity-method losses -- all of which this model already charges or excludes explicitly elsewhere. The comparable multiples across these restructurings are EV/EBITDA and P/Sales, and both came in BELOW their ten-year historical range after the fix (11.4x vs a 12.97x floor; 2.77x vs a 2.83x floor). Clearing the P/E rule mechanically would require cutting the base value a further ~7%; the fix was stopped after one pass as the protocol requires. The ~62% weighted upside should be read against the bear case -- the equity is a levered stub and the dispersion, not the midpoint, is the finding.
